title: One ten-thousandth apart
hook: The rule is exact. The two starts differ by 0.0001. Where are they after 30 steps?

knows: an exact rule gives exact predictions
doesNotKnow: that in a chaotic system a tiny difference in the start roughly doubles each step
so making the start more precise buys only a few more steps of forecast

misconception: If the rule is known exactly, a tiny measurement error stays tiny.
objective: The learner can explain that under the exact rule x → 4x(1 − x) two starts 0.0001 apart split by step 11, that a start 1,000 times more precise splits only 10 steps later because the gap roughly doubles each step, and that chaos limits forecasting a particular step, not the long-run average.

claims.text: Under x → 4x(1 − x), runs from 0.3 and 0.3001 first differ by more than 0.1 at step 11 and are 0.616 apart at step 30; runs from 0.3 and 0.3000001 (1,000 times more precise) first differ by more than 0.1 at step 21, 10 steps later.
claims.source: Direct iteration in double precision: company/domains/briefs/checks/big-ideas-cycle1-check.mjs (brief #6 and the W-537 block); Demo.tsx series() and splitStep() compute every point and marker on the stage. Re-run by the builder in node, 2026-10-14: 11, 21, gap 0.616 at step 30.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Re-iterated x -> 4x(1 - x) in node (own code, double precision): gap 0.0001 first exceeds 0.1 at step 11, gap at step 30 = 0.616; gap 0.0000001 first exceeds 0.1 at step 21, 10 steps later. Matches Demo.tsx splitStep()/series() and the reveal ('until step 11', 'only 10 more steps').

claims.text: In this map the gap between two nearby runs roughly doubles each step.
claims.source: The r = 4 logistic map is conjugate to the doubling (tent) map, so its Lyapunov exponent is ln 2: small gaps grow by a factor of about 2 per step on average. Consistent with the stage: a 1,000× smaller gap (log2 1000 ≈ 10) buys 10 steps (c1). Standard result, e.g. Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, 2nd ed., ch. 10 (not needed for the derivation; not opened by the builder).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation plus numeric check: x = sin^2(pi theta) conjugates the r = 4 map to theta -> 2 theta mod 1, so the Lyapunov exponent is ln 2 and small gaps grow by about 2 per step on average. Node: mean of ln|4 - 8x| over 1e6 steps = 0.693146 (ln 2 = 0.693147). Consistent with c1: log2(1000) = 9.97, about 10 steps. Strogatz not opened and not needed. The recall's log2(100) = 6.64, about 7 days, also re-checked.

Not opened by the builder. (support: convention, a definition).

claims.text: Where it stops: each step was unpredictable, but the long-run averages matched (0.51 from 0.3 and 0.48 from 0.3001, over 1,000 steps); chaos limits forecasting a particular step, not the average.
claims.source: 1,000-step averages computed in Demo.tsx longAverage() and in the cycle-1 check script (W-537 block): 0.51 and 0.48. The exact long-run mean of the r = 4 map is 0.5 (its invariant density is 1/(π√(x(1 − x))), symmetric about 0.5). Shown on the stage by the 'Average 1,000 steps' preset (strategy D4 a: the limit is shown, not told). The reveal has a second branch for learners who did not press 'Average 1,000 steps': 'Where it stops: chaos limits forecasting a particular day, not necessarily the average. Average 1,000 steps compares the two runs' long-run averages.' It quotes no values. The brief's last sentence ('That is why a forecast fades after days…') was cut for the 90-word budget; it would have been a second weather claim resting on c3.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Node: 1,000-step averages from 0.3 and 0.3001 = 0.5119 and 0.4810, shown 0.51 and 0.48 (toFixed(2)). Exact long-run mean: the invariant density 1/(pi sqrt(x(1 - x))) is symmetric about 1/2, so the mean is 0.5. 'Matched' is fair: both are within about 0.02 of 0.5 while single steps differ by up to 1. The no-average branch of the reveal states no value and holds.

claims.text: The rule, the start 0.3 and the gaps 0.0001 and 0.0000001 are the lesson's choices; every value of the map stays between 0 and 1, so two unrelated runs can be up to 1 apart.
claims.source: The lesson's model (brief #6). For x in [0, 1], 4x(1 − x) is in [0, 1]. Option C's 'like two random numbers' is a description of the runs' behaviour after they split, not a claim that the map is random.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Convention: start 0.3 and gaps 1e-4 and 1e-7 are constants in Demo.tsx (X_START, COARSE, FINE). For x in [0, 1], 4x(1 - x) has maximum 1 at x = 1/2 and minimum 0, so every value stays in [0, 1] and two runs are at most 1 apart.

recall.question: A forecast's error doubles every day. If today's measurements were 100 times more precise, how much longer would the forecast stay useful?
recall.why: An error that doubles daily takes log2(100) ≈ 6.6 more doublings to grow from 100 times smaller back to the same size, so precision buys about a week, not 100 times as long.
